v.why: With edge 3 already an identity, a skip on edge 5 adds redundant identity while removing the deep path's final transform, so it hurts more.
Parallel identity routes into node 3 substitute for each other, so a second skip adds no new signal and dilutes the learned contribution.
A skip on edge 3 complements a conv-terminated deep path to form a clean residual block, the motif of top NAS-Bench-201 cells.
When edge 3 already supplies a conv path into node 3, a pooling branch on edge 4 replaces less needed capacity and hurts less.
With edge 4 removed, node 3 has fewer incoming paths, so a conv on edge 3 adds a larger share of the cell's learned output.
Edge 2 only matters if node 1 carries signal; the contrast includes edge 0 = none where node 1 is zero, and stacked convs compound, so the edge-2 conv gains more when edge 0 is a conv.
Features from an edge-0 conv are exploited by a learned edge-4 transform into node 3, whereas when edge 4 is none or parameter-free node 1's contribution to the output is weaker.
A conv on edge 1 keeps learned features flowing into node 2, so replacing edge 2 with a pool costs less.
With edge 2 removed, edge 1 is node 2's sole input, so its operation fully determines node 2's features and a conv there matters more.
Removing edge 3 when edge 5 is already gone leaves node 3 fed only by edge 4, so path removal compounds and hurts much more.

- **e1 conv | e5 none** and **e2 conv | e5 none:** node 2 has no path to the output.

None of the candidates uses the edited edge's own value as its condition.
